candidates.attacker_control: The GET /oauth/authorize 'scope' request parameter is fully attacker-chosen. DefaultOAuth2RequestFactory.createAuthorizationRequest/extractScopes parse it into the AuthorizationRequest scope set (DefaultOAuth2RequestFactory.java:69-88,125-140); AuthorizationEndpoint.authorize stores the request in the model and forwards to the approval page (AuthorizationEndpoint.java:123,180-182,241-247). With the default annotation-configured authorization server (non-JWT token store), an ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler with a TokenApprovalStore is selected by default (AuthorizationServerEndpointsConfigurer.java:444-455,477-498) and its getUserApprovalRequest publishes a "scopes" map whose keys are 'scope.' + each requested scope name (ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler.java:233-244). WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint then substitutes those keys into the SpEL template, so a scope string that survives parameter parsing and scope validation is interpreted as an expression.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked and recorded as limiting factors rather than dismissing the lead: (a) DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator enforces scope subset-of-client unless client scopes are null/empty, so a malicious scope normally requires a client registered with that scope (e.g. self-service/dynamic client registration) or a client with no scopes configured; this is the main exploitability caveat. (b) The OAuth2 XML namespace path defaults to DefaultUserApprovalHandler (AuthorizationServerBeanDefinitionParser.java:260-263), which does not add a "scopes" map, so the whitelabel page there has no scope list; the annotation config path is the default that does populate it. (c) JwtTokenStore disables the default approval store (AuthorizationServerEndpointsConfigurer.java:453-455), removing the "scopes" map in JWT setups. (d) The whitelabel error page was checked: errorSummary is HTML-escaped and put in the model (WhitelabelErrorEndpoint.java:27-38), not concatenated into the template, so no expression re-entry. (e) SpelView is referenced only by these two endpoints (grep for new SpelView). (f) JwtHelper.decodeAndVerify always verifies with the configured verifier and does not select an algorithm from the token header, so no alg-confusion/none bypass found there. (g) JdbcClientDetailsService/JdbcTokenStore/JdbcApprovalStore use parameterized SQL (checked string-built SQL patterns). (h) Refresh-token scope narrowing is validated in DefaultTokenServices.createRefreshedAuthentication and TokenEndpoint validates scopes for token requests. (i) No escaping/sanitization of '${' or scope values exists anywhere in the approval-page path (grep for escape/HtmlUtils/'${').
candidates.impact: Server-side evaluation of attacker-influenced SpEL in the authorization-server JVM. Because the evaluation context is a plain StandardEvaluationContext, type references (T(...)) and reflection are available, so successful injection enables arbitrary method invocation and command execution in the authorization server process, i.e. full compromise of the authorization server and the credentials/tokens it holds. Even without code execution, injected expressions expose model/server state in the approval page. The defect is a classic template-then-evaluate ordering flaw (user data concatenated into a template that is later parsed as an expression).
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The default whitelabel approval page is used (no custom /oauth/confirm_access controller) and the configured UserApprovalHandler publishes a "scopes" map (default ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler for @EnableAuthorizationServer with a non-JWT token store; also any custom handler that adds "scopes", or a request attribute "scopes"). 2) The craftable scope string must pass DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.validateScope: it must be one of the client's registered scopes, OR the client must have an empty/null scope set (membership check is skipped in that case, DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.java:27-39). 3) The client must not auto-approve that scope (otherwise checkForPreApproval skips the page). 4) An authenticated user must be induced to send the crafted authorize request (client_id, response_type=code|token, redirect_uri, malicious scope). 5) Payload must avoid characters split by OAuth2Utils.parseParameterList ('[\s+]', i.e. whitespace and '+') - trivially satisfiable.
candidates.root_cause: WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.createScopes() builds the approval-page HTML by substituting the keys of the model's "scopes" map (which are scope names, prefixed with "scope.") verbatim into the %scope% and %key% markers of the SCOPE template fragment (WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.java:46-60). The assembled template is then passed to SpelView, whose constructor installs a PropertyPlaceholderHelper with prefix "${" and suffix "}" and a resolver that calls new SpelExpressionParser().parseExpression(name).getValue(context) (SpelView.java:47-57); render() runs the resolver over the whole template (SpelView.java:64-74). Because scope names are placed into the template *before* placeholder resolution and nothing escapes "${" / "}" or restricts the evaluation context (StandardEvaluationContext with MapAccessor, T() type references and reflection enabled), a scope name containing something like ${T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...)} is compiled and evaluated as a SpEL expression on the server when the approval page renders. The same pattern exists only for the approval page; the whitelabel error page uses a static template and resolves an HTML-escaped summary from the model (WhitelabelErrorEndpoint.java:21-39), so it does not re-enter template syntax.
candidates.title: SpEL expression injection in whitelabel OAuth2 approval page via attacker-influenced scope names (potential RCE)
candidates.trace: GET /oauth/authorize?client_id=<client>&response_type=code&redirect_uri=...&scope=<payload> -> AuthorizationEndpoint.authorize -> getOAuth2RequestFactory().createAuthorizationRequest(parameters) extracts scopes from the 'scope' parameter (DefaultOAuth2RequestFactory.java:69-88,125-140) -> oauth2RequestValidator.validateScope(...) (AuthorizationEndpoint.java:156) -> userApprovalHandler.checkForPreApproval/isApproved -> model.put("authorizationRequest", ...) and getUserApprovalPageResponse -> forward:/oauth/confirm_access (AuthorizationEndpoint.java:180-182,241-247) -> ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler.getUserApprovalRequest adds "scopes" map keyed 'scope.'+scope (ApprovalStoreUserApprovalHandler.java:228-246) -> WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.getAccessConfirmation -> createTemplate -> createScopes substitutes raw scope keys into %scope%/%key% (WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint.java:29-60) -> new SpelView(template) (line 26) -> SpelView.render -> PropertyPlaceholderHelper("${","}") finds the injected placeholder -> parser.parseExpression(name).getValue(context) executes the embedded SpEL with StandardEvaluationContext (SpelView.java:47-74).
candidates.unverified: Not executed; no runtime confirmation. The exact deployment configuration that would let an attacker obtain a client whose registered scope contains a SpEL payload (or a client with an empty scope set) was not verified, and the snapshot contains no tests or git history to confirm the intended fix. Whether the historical upstream fix for this component changed this file, SpelView, or the approval handler could not be checked offline, so the finding is expressed as the source-visible injection path rather than a confirmed exploitable RCE.
candidates.weakness_type: Expression Language Injection (CWE-917) leading to Code Injection / RCE (CWE-94)

coverage_summary: Enumerated all 445 visible source files (get_source_scope reports no excluded/sensitive/symlink/binary filtering beyond NUL-byte handling; no test sources are present in the snapshot). Deep review of the OAuth2 authorization-server path: AuthorizationEndpoint (authorize/approveOrDeny, redirect and implicit-code responses), WhitelabelApprovalEndpoint + SpelView + WhitelabelErrorEndpoint, ApprovalStore/TokenStore/Default user-approval handlers, DefaultOAuth2RequestFactory/Validator, AuthorizationRequest/BaseRequest/OAuth2Request, TokenEndpoint, TokenEndpointAuthenticationFilter, ClientCredentialsTokenEndpointFilter, CheckTokenEndpoint/TokenKeyEndpoint, DefaultTokenServices refresh and load paths, DefaultRedirectResolver/ExactMatchRedirectResolver, JWT converter/token store and spring-security-jwt JwtHelper/codec/signers, resource-server authentication filters (BearerTokenExtractor, OAuth2AuthenticationManager, OAuth2AuthenticationProcessingFilter), annotation and XML configuration classes, and JDBC/Redis token/client/approval stores at a targeted level. Modules/files reviewed only by search/spot-check (not exhaustively): OAuth1 provider and consumer packages, samples (sparklr/tonr), docs, code-style files, and small utility classes.
limitations: No execution, tests, scanners, or exploitation performed; findings are source-level only and not runtime-confirmed.
The snapshot has no test sources and no git history, so the exact intended fix/parent commit and the upstream fix shape could not be verified locally.

Exploitability of the SpEL candidate depends on deployment configuration (whitelabel approval page in use, an ApprovalStore-backed user-approval handler, and a client whose registered scopes contain the payload or whose scope set is empty); this was not confirmed for any concrete deployment.
OAuth1 provider/consumer internals, JDBC/Redis store serialization details, samples, and docs were only spot-checked, so additional issues could exist there.

The bot-limited files (5 MiB cap, NUL-byte skip) did not exclude any files per get_source_scope; however, generated artifacts, native binaries, and any files outside the assigned tree were not available.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultRedirectResolver accepts any requested redirect_uri when the client has no registered redirect URIs, and otherwise matches subdomains/path prefixes rather than requiring an exact registered URI (DefaultRedirectResolver.java:63-86,112-125).
rejected_leads.reason: Real weak validation with open-redirect/authorization-code theft potential, but it is a long-standing design behavior gated on client registration data (no registered URI, or a registered host/path that the attacker can shadow); less source-level evidence of an outright injectable flaw than the SpEL path, and it is a separate root cause that was not selected under the one-candidate cap.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator skips scope membership validation entirely when the client has no scopes (DefaultOAuth2RequestValidator.java:27-39).
rejected_leads.reason: Not reported separately: it is a precondition that widens the SpEL-injection path rather than an independent impact; the primary candidate's trace already notes it.

rejected_leads.lead: XSS / expression concerns in the whitelabel error page (WhitelabelErrorEndpoint.java).
rejected_leads.reason: The error summary is HTML-escaped and placed in the model, and the template is static; no user data is concatenated into the SpEL template there.

rejected_leads.lead: JWT parsing in JwtHelper/JwtAccessTokenConverter (header alg not used for verifier selection, empty crypto segment handling).
rejected_leads.reason: decodeAndVerify always applies the configured SignatureVerifier; the header alg is not used to choose verification, so no none/alg-confusion bypass was identified from source. The spring-security-jwt module is also commented out of the parent build.

rejected_leads.lead: RedisTokenStore JDK serialization (JdkSerializationStrategy) deserializes Java objects from Redis.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires write access to the Redis data store, which is outside the reviewed trust boundary; no attacker-controlled path from HTTP endpoints into the deserializer was established.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth1 provider signature handling (OAuthProviderProcessingFilter, PlainTextSignatureMethod, CoreOAuthSignatureMethodFactory).
rejected_leads.reason: Spot-checked only; nothing concrete identified in the time available, and PLAINTEXT is an opt-in configuration. Not sufficient evidence for a candidate.

summary: Repository: spring-security-oauth, parent version 2.0.10.BUILD-SNAPSHOT (spring-security-oauth OAuth1, spring-security-oauth2, spring-security-jwt [module commented out of the build], samples, docs). I enumerated the 445 visible files and deep-read the OAuth2 authorization-server request path, approval handlers, SpEL view rendering, request factory/validator, annotation + XML configuration wiring, redirect resolution, token services/refresh path, JWT converter, resource-server filters and OAuth1 filter spot checks. The single strongest candidate is a SpEL expression injection in the default (whitelabel) OAuth2 approval page: scope names taken from the authorization request are interpolated verbatim into an HTML template string that is subsequently compiled and evaluated by SpelView with an unrestricted StandardEvaluationContext (T() type references reachable), which can lead to server-side code execution when the page is rendered. This matches a critical class of issue historically reported against this exact component in the 2.0.x line. All other reviewed leads were weaker or already mitigated; no additional candidates are submitted.
